\chapter{How Are You}
\label{ch:how-are-you}
\hlchaptermodality{8}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask a stranger how they are.}

Greeting plus the question that opens almost every conversation.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[estar]{estar — \textquotedblleft{}to be,\textquotedblright{} the \emph{standing} kind}

\label{lesson:ES-C04-estar}



\begin{quote}
To ask \emph{how are you?} Spanish needs a verb for \textbf{being}. Today just the verb itself and where it came from; how to use it, and its two forms, come next.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{st-no-e} — Spanish never starts a word with a bare \emph{st-}; it props it up with an \emph{e}: \emph{es-TAR}. (That reflex is why Spanish speakers say \emph{e-Spain}, \emph{e-student} — the same \emph{e} that Latin \emph{stāre} grew to become \emph{estar}.)
  \item \texttt{r-tap} — the final \emph{r} is one soft tap: \emph{es-TAR}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{estar} comes straight from Latin \textbf{stāre}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}to stand.\textquotedblright{}} Hold onto that picture: it is the whole reason this verb behaves the way it does. How you are \textbf{standing} at this moment — well, tired, here, there — is a snapshot, not a permanent fact.

That root \textbf{stā-/sta-} is one of the most productive in English. \emph{Estar} hands you a large family for free:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{stay}, \textbf{stand}, \textbf{stance}, \textbf{station}, \textbf{stable}, \textbf{stationary} — to stand or stay put.
  \item \textbf{state}, \textbf{status}, \textbf{statue}, \textbf{estate} — a way of \emph{standing} (your state is how you stand).
  \item \textbf{constant}, \textbf{circumstance}, \textbf{substance} — \textquotedblleft{}standing with / around / under.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

So \emph{¿cómo estás?} is, at the root, \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}how are you standing?\textquotedblright{}}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}estar\textquotedblright{} — \emph{es-TAR}, with the little propping \emph{e}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}estar\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}stay, state, status, stable\textquotedblright{} — all \emph{standing}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Latin verb is \emph{estar} — \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}to stand\textquotedblright{}? (To \textbf{stand} — \emph{stāre}.) Why does Spanish put an \emph{e} on the front? (It never begins a word with bare \emph{st-}.) Name two English cousins. (\emph{Stay, state, status, stable, estate}…) Next: the two forms you will actually ask with.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[estás / está]{estás / está — the two forms, and what they are for}

\label{lesson:ES-C04-estar-estado}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Estar} is \textquotedblleft{}to stand.\textquotedblright{} Now put it to work. Two forms, one job: saying how somebody is \textbf{right now}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item estar — the verb and its Latin \textquotedblleft{}to stand\textquotedblright{} root.
  \item tú \emph{or} usted — why \emph{usted} takes he/she forms.
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: state and location use estar}]
Use \textbf{estar} for a \textbf{current state} or a \textbf{location} — the two things that can change without changing what something \emph{is}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a state: \emph{estoy bien} — \textquotedblleft{}I'm well\textquotedblright{} (today; maybe not tomorrow).
  \item a location: \emph{está aquí} — \textquotedblleft{}it's here\textquotedblright{} (for now).
\end{itemize}

\textquotedblleft{}How are you?\textquotedblright{} asks about a current state, so it takes \emph{estar}. Spanish has a second be-verb for identity, and it arrives in its own later lesson; keeping it out of today's drill lets one contrast settle at a time.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the two forms you need}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{you're addressing} & \textbf{form} & \textbf{reads as} \\
\midrule
\textbf{tú} (informal) & \textbf{estás} & \textquotedblleft{}you are\textquotedblright{} \\
\textbf{usted} (formal) & \textbf{está} & \textquotedblleft{}you are\textquotedblright{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Notice that \textbf{está} is also \textquotedblleft{}he is / she is.\textquotedblright{} That is not a coincidence and not something extra to learn — it is the \emph{usted}-takes-he/she-forms rule you already met, showing up for the first time in a real verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}estás\textquotedblright{} … \textquotedblleft{}está\textquotedblright{} — the two forms you'll ask with
  \item which one goes with \emph{tú}, which with \emph{usted}
  \item a state, then a location — \textquotedblleft{}estás bien\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}está aquí\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two kinds of thing does \emph{estar} cover? (\textbf{Current state} and \textbf{location}.) Which form goes with \emph{tú}, and which with \emph{usted}? (\emph{Estás}; \emph{está}.) Why is \emph{está} also \textquotedblleft{}he/she is\textquotedblright{}? (Because \emph{usted} takes the \textbf{he/she} verb forms.) Next lesson, you finally ask it: \textbf{¿cómo está usted?}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[¿cómo está usted?]{¿cómo está usted? — \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C04-como-esta}



\begin{quote}
Everything you've built this chapter now snaps together into one question. You already met \textbf{cómo} (\textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{}) and the \textbf{tú / usted} choice back in when you first met them; you just learned \textbf{estar}. Assemble them.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{¿Cómo está usted?} = \textquotedblleft{}How are you?\textquotedblright{} (formal) literally: \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}In what manner are you standing?\textquotedblright{}}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{cómo} = \textquotedblleft{}how / in what manner\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{está} = \textquotedblleft{}you are\textquotedblright{} (the \emph{usted}/he-she form of \textbf{estar} — state, not identity)
  \item \textbf{usted} = the formal \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

Note the \textbf{¿} — Spanish opens a question with an upside-down mark so you know the melody is coming before you start reading aloud. (We take that mark apart in a dedicated writing lesson.)
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¿Cómo está usted?\textquotedblright{} — formal, for a stranger
  \item the pieces — \textquotedblleft{}cómo + está + usted\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which be-verb does \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} use — \emph{ser} or \emph{estar}, and why? (\emph{estar} — it's about your current state.) What changes between formal and informal? (\textbf{The next step changes the ending and pronoun.}) Next: choosing the register.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{How are you — putting the question together}

\label{lesson:ES-C04-repaso-como-esta}



\begin{quote}
You have a second \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} and the question it carries. Nothing new here — only what you already have.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\begin{quote}
— Buenos días. \textbf{¿Cómo está usted?}
\end{quote}

The answer is the next chapter. Asking is this one.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can ask a stranger how they are, which is the question that opens almost every conversation you will ever have in Spanish.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¿Cómo está usted?\textquotedblright{} — to someone you have just met
  \item the greeting and the question together, as one breath
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} carries how someone is, and why? (\emph{Estar} — a state, not an identity.) Ask the question once more from memory.
\end{tcolorbox}
